prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: Sakshi discussed about (1) / the problem with (2) / her manager very briefly. (3) / No Error (4)
explanation: 'Discuss' is a transitive verb and takes a direct object without any preposition; 'discussed about' is wrong, so it should be 'Sakshi discussed'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: If there had not been (1) / such a long queue (2) / I could have returned back by 11 am. (3) / No Error (4)
options: I could have returned back by 11 am.
explanation: 'Return' already conveys the sense of coming back, so 'returned back' is redundant; write 'I could have returned by 11 am.'

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: This happened (a) / just exactly (b) / five years ago (c) / No error (d)
explanation: 'Just' and 'exactly' carry the same meaning here, so using both is redundant; use either 'just five years ago' or 'exactly five years ago'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: It was a big blunder (a) / but we ignored it (b) / for the welfare of the city. (c) / No error (d)
options: for the welfare of the city.
explanation: A 'blunder' is by definition a big/serious mistake, so 'big blunder' is redundant; say 'It was a blunder'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: If anybody is found (1) / to violate against the laws (2) / of this country, he will be given severe punishment. (3) / No error (4)
options: of this country, he will be given severe punishment.
explanation: 'Violate' is transitive and needs no preposition, so 'violate against the laws' is wrong; it should be 'to violate the laws'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: I will spend / my rest of remaining / life in my / native village.
explanation: 'Rest' and 'remaining' mean the same thing, making the phrase redundant; the correct form is 'the rest of my life' (or 'my remaining life').

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: Your name / precedes before mine / in the / admission list.
explanation: 'Precede' already means 'to come before', so 'before' is superfluous; write 'precedes mine'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: Within an hour's journey we (a) / will approach near (b) / Patna, (c) / No error (d)
explanation: 'Approach' is a transitive verb taking a direct object, so 'near' is unnecessary; it should be 'will approach Patna'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: Supposing if all your problems (a) / had been solved, (b) / what would you have done? (c) / No Error (d)
explanation: 'Supposing' itself introduces the condition, so adding 'if' duplicates it; use either 'Supposing all your problems...' or 'If all your problems...'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: He denied that he was not (a) / present on the spot of (b) / the occurrence, (c) / No Error (d)
options: He denied that he was not
explanation: 'Denied' already carries a negative sense, so 'not' creates a double negative; it should be 'He denied that he was present'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: My father asked me if I had (a) / sufficient enough money (b) / to pay the fees, (c) / no error (d)
options: My father asked me if I had
explanation: 'Sufficient' and 'enough' are synonyms, so using both is redundant; write 'sufficient money' or 'enough money'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The candidate requested the Chairman (a) / to repeat the (b) / question again, (c) / no error (d)
explanation: 'Repeat' means to say again, so 'again' is redundant; it should simply be 'to repeat the question'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The Principal forbade (a) / the students not to (b) / stage a walk out. (c) / no error (d)
explanation: 'Forbid' already expresses prohibition, so 'not to' makes it a double negative; the correct form is 'forbade the students to stage a walk out'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: In Delhi, he came across with many (a) / of his friends (b) / who had settled there, (c) / no error (d)
options: In Delhi, he came across with many
explanation: 'Come across' means to meet by chance and is followed directly by the object, so 'with' must be dropped: 'he came across many of his friends'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: Probably by the end (a) / of the year he will (b) / leave for the USA with bag and baggage, (c) / no error (d)
options: leave for the USA with bag and baggage,
explanation: The idiom is 'bag and baggage' used adverbially without a preposition, so 'with' is wrong: 'leave for the USA bag and baggage'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: Two recent incidents (a) / amply illustrate about the present political (b) / condition of the country, (c) / no error (d)
options: amply illustrate about the present political
explanation: 'Illustrate' is transitive and takes a direct object without a preposition, so it should be 'amply illustrate the present political condition'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: Supposing if it rains heavily (A) / on the day of the exam, (B) / will the scheduled session be postponed? (C) / No Error (D)
explanation: 'Supposing' already functions as a conditional conjunction, so 'if' is redundant: use 'Supposing it rains heavily' or 'If it rains heavily'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The weather condition today (A) / is comparatively hotter than it was (B) / during the exact same period last week. (C) / No Error (D)
options: is comparatively hotter than it was (B)
during the exact same period last week. (C)
explanation: 'Comparatively' cannot be used with a comparative followed by 'than'; write 'is hotter than it was' (or 'is comparatively hot').

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The sudden heavy downpour coped up with (A) / the infrastructure challenges, exposing the municipal (B) / corporation's total lack of urban flood preparedness. (C) / No Error (D)
options: The sudden heavy downpour coped up with
the infrastructure challenges, exposing the municipal
corporation's total lack of urban flood preparedness.
explanation: 'Cope' takes only 'with' — the particle 'up' is redundant; write 'The sudden heavy downpour coped with the infrastructure challenges' (correctly, 'compounded').

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The reason why he was rejected (A) / from the final campus placement rounds (B) / was because his communication skills were inadequate. (C) / No Error (D)
options: The reason why he was rejected
from the final campus placement rounds
was because his communication skills were inadequate.
explanation: 'The reason... was because' is redundant; use 'was that' — 'was that his communication skills were inadequate'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The suspect denied that (A) / he had not stolen the corporate layout designs (B) / from the research database vault. (C) / No Error (D)
options: he had not stolen the corporate layout designs
explanation: 'Denied' already carries the negative sense, so 'had not stolen' creates a double negative; it should read 'denied that he had stolen the corporate layout designs'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The international diplomatic mission (A) / returned back to their home country (B) / after the peace talk rounds collapsed. (C) / No Error (D)
options: returned back to their home country
after the peace talk rounds collapsed.
explanation: 'Returned back' is redundant since 'return' already means to go back; use 'returned to their home country'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: I requested the senior flight attendant (A) / to kindly repeat the safety evacuation (B) / announcement once again. (C) / No Error (D)
options: I requested the senior flight attendant
to kindly repeat the safety evacuation
explanation: 'Repeat' already means to say something again, so 'once again' is redundant; end the sentence at 'announcement'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: In my opinion, I think (A) / the newly proposed real estate project (B) / will struggle to attract premium home buyers. (C) / No Error (D)
options: the newly proposed real estate project
will struggle to attract premium home buyers.
explanation: 'In my opinion' and 'I think' express the same idea, so using both is redundant; keep only one, e.g. 'In my opinion, the newly proposed...'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The multi-national enterprise (A) / will advance forward with its expansion (B) / plans despite the global financial slump. (C) / No Error (D)
options: will advance forward with its expansion
plans despite the global financial slump.
explanation: 'Advance forward' is redundant because 'advance' means to move forward; write 'will advance with its expansion plans'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The technical committee members (A) / unanimously agreed together on the final choice (B) / of the software vendor platform. (C) / No Error (D)
options: unanimously agreed together on the final choice
explanation: 'Agreed together' is redundant since agreement is already mutual; use 'unanimously agreed on the final choice'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The operational supervisor ordered (A) / the immediate cancellation of the evening shift (B) / due to a reason of sudden power failure. (C) / No Error (D)
explanation: 'Due to a reason of' is redundant because 'due to' already gives the reason; write 'due to a sudden power failure'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The investigative panel stated (A) / that the two cross-border trade agreements (B) / were completely identical to each other in every aspect. (C) / No Error (D)
explanation: 'Identical' is an absolute term, so 'completely' and 'in every aspect' are redundant; write 'were identical to each other'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The design layout of the new sedan (A) / is both aesthetically appealing to the eye (B) / and aerodynamically highly efficient. (C) / No Error (D)
explanation: 'Aesthetically appealing to the eye' is redundant because 'aesthetically' already conveys visual appeal; write simply 'is both aesthetically appealing'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The operations executive requested the clients (A) / to assemble together inside the main conference (B) / hall room for the annual presentation session. (C) / No Error (D)
explanation: 'Assemble' already means to gather in one place, so 'together' is redundant; use 'to assemble inside the main conference hall'.

prompt: Identify the segment in the sentence which contains the grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'
sentence: Those who are late they will not be allowed inside the classroom.
explanation: The relative clause 'Those who are late' already supplies the subject, so the extra pronoun 'they' is superfluous; it should be 'will not be allowed'.

sentence: Parts of the following sentence are given as options. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. The reason for visiting Meerut was because my mother needed to be looked after.
explanation: 'The reason ... was because' is redundant; the correct construction is 'The reason ... was that'.

prompt: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
sentence: Your name / precedes before / mine / in the list.
explanation: 'Precede' already means 'come before', so 'before' is superfluous: 'Your name precedes mine'.

prompt: Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, then select the option "No error".
sentence: And it just recently awarded/ a million-dollar contract/ that reeks of corruption.
explanation: 'Just' and 'recently' convey the same idea, making 'just recently' redundant; one of the two adverbs should be dropped.

prompt: Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.
sentence: He wanted to know / the reason / why his low score / in Mathematics.
explanation: 'Why' must introduce a clause with a finite verb; with only a noun phrase the correct form is 'for his low score'.

sentence: Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error. My father is comparatively better today.
explanation: 'Comparatively' with the comparative 'better' is redundant; correct forms are 'comparatively well' or simply 'better today'.

prompt: Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
sentence: What the council could not anticipate (1)/ was that the regulatory changes, sudden as they seemed, (2)/ were in fact a culmination of several years (3)/ of there being dissatisfaction within the sector. (4)
explanation: 'There being' is a superfluous expletive construction; the phrase should read 'of dissatisfaction within the sector'.

prompt: Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
sentence: She speaks more persuasively than she writes, (1)/ which, according to her critics, (2)/ makes her a better orator rather than (3)/ an accomplished communicator. (4)
explanation: The comparative 'better' must be completed by 'than' alone; 'rather' is superfluous — 'a better orator than an accomplished communicator'.

prompt: Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error’.
sentence: The front part is used for carving / the lines and the back end / for scratching of whole areas.
options: the lines and the back end
The front part is used for carving
explanation: The gerund 'scratching' takes a direct object, so the preposition 'of' is superfluous: 'for scratching whole areas'.

prompt: Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select "No error’.
sentence: Eddie just panics/ when it gets close/ nearer the end.
explanation: 'Close' and 'nearer' together are redundant; it should be 'when it gets close to the end' (or 'nearer the end').

prompt: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
sentence: He climbed of / the steep mountain trail, / his backpack heavy / with supplies for the journey.
explanation: 'Climb' is used transitively here and needs no preposition: 'He climbed the steep mountain trail'.

prompt: Select the alternative that will improve the underlined part of the sentence in case
sentence: there is no improvement select “No improvement” I am very much pleased to see you here today.
explanation: 'very much' before the participial adjective 'pleased' is superfluous; 'very pleased' is the standard form.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
sentence: Computers and mobile phones have become a necessary and important part of our lives.
explanation: 'Necessary and important' is redundant; the single adjective 'an essential part' conveys the same meaning concisely.

prompt: Choose the option that can substitute the underlined segment correctly and complete
sentence: the meaning of the sentence. Navika is a superb and impressive child in her class.
explanation: 'Brilliant' correctly describes an outstanding child, whereas 'superb and impressive' is redundant and the other options describe things, not a child's ability.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select No improvement.
sentence: They started playing badminton at a young age of nine years old .
options: the young age of nine years old
a young age of nine years
explanation: The fixed phrase is 'at the young age of nine'; 'years old' after the number is superfluous.

prompt: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case
sentence: no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. It is the true fact that the second wave of Covid-19 that has gripped India is more deadly.
explanation: 'True fact' is redundant since a fact is by definition true, so 'a fact' is the correct concise form.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
sentence: As I have no time to discuss the points, so I wrote a email to her.
options: so I wrote an e-mail for her
so I wrote a e-mail to her
I write an email to her
I wrote an email to her
explanation: When a sentence begins with 'As', the correlative 'so' is superfluous; also 'an email' is required before the vowel sound.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution’.
sentence: Accordingly to my opinion your essay is the best.
explanation: The correct idiom is 'According to me'; 'accordingly to' is wrong and 'according to my opinion' is redundant since 'according to' already conveys opinion.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution’.
sentence: He went to foreign for higher education.
explanation: 'Abroad' is an adverb meaning 'to a foreign country', so no preposition is used: 'went abroad'.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
sentence: Ratul’s capability of being able to speak two languages is apt for this post.
explanation: The wordy phrase 'capability of being able to speak two languages' is redundant and is concisely expressed by 'bilingual'.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
sentence: Rajan’s caused extremely painful headaches.
explanation: 'Excruciating' single-handedly conveys 'extremely painful', removing the wordy phrase.

sentence: A part of the following sentence is highlighted. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel Options A, B, or C do not improve the sentence, then choose Option D: "No Improvement Required." The doctor warned that the patient tends to lapse back into his old dietary habits after every period of supervised recovery.
options: lapse into his old dietary habits
lapse backward into his old dietary habits
lapse back again into his old dietary habits
explanation: 'Lapse' already conveys falling back, so 'back' is superfluous; 'lapse into his old dietary habits' is correct.

sentence: A part of the following sentence is highlighted. Choose the option that best replaces the highlighted part to improve the sentence. If no improvement is needed, choose 'No improvement required'. The committee decided to move forward ahead with the new infrastructure plan despite objections.
explanation: 'Forward' and 'ahead' express the same idea, so one is redundant; 'move forward with' is correct.
